comparison: Perfect agreement on dataset claims (C1, C2, C11, C12, C75, C76, C77). Both evaluations find the dataset size, scope, and collection methods well-documented and supported. OpenEval emphasizes explicit documentation while peer reviewers characterize it as 'large' and 'rich' with 'solid methodology.'

Perfect agreement on baseline self-citation rates (C14-C18). Both evaluations find these descriptive statistics convincing and well-supported with appropriate confidence intervals and statistical tests.

Perfect agreement on temporal trends (C3, C19-C22). Both evaluations accept the finding of diverging patterns between First and Last Authors over time, with OpenEval noting robust statistical evidence and peer reviewers finding it convincing as one of four key findings.

Perfect agreement on career stage analysis (C23, C24, C55). Both evaluations support the finding that First and Last Authors show comparable self-citation rates at the same academic age, with appropriate visual evidence.

Perfect agreement on geographic differences (C4, C25-C27, C45-C46). Both evaluations accept the geographic patterns and correlation with publication history. OpenEval provides detailed statistical support while peer reviewers accept it as one of four key findings.

Perfect agreement on field-specific patterns (C6, C28-C32). Both evaluations support the LDA topic modeling approach and resulting subfield differences. OpenEval notes some subjective interpretation in topic assignments while peer reviewers find the evidence convincing.

Divergent evaluations on interpretive claims (C51-C54). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculations not directly tested and that C52's career impact claim lacks empirical demonstration. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting them as reasonable interpretations without critique.

Perfect agreement on study limitations (C66-C70). Both evaluations support these acknowledged limitations as appropriate and important caveats, with peer reviewers noting they were addressed in revision.

Perfect agreement on citation diversity reporting (C89-C90). Both evaluations support this transparency practice, with OpenEval commending the self-reflection and peer reviewers implicitly accepting it without comment.

Agreement on gender differences (C33-C44 in OpenEval; C5, C33-C44, C59-C60 in peer review). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes concerns about projection assumptions while accepting raw differences. Peer reviewers accept the nuanced interpretation that differences stem from publication counts rather than behavior.

Strong agreement on GAM model findings (C47-C49 in OpenEval; C47-C50 in peer review). Both evaluations support these model-derived insights. Peer reviewers include C50 (gender effects controlled by publication count) while OpenEval addresses this separately in R9.

Partial overlap on gender mechanism (C5, C60, C50 in OpenEval; C5, C59, C60 in peer review subset). Both support the finding that gender effects largely disappear when controlling for publication history. OpenEval emphasizes this as a key mechanistic insight with appropriate statistical modeling.

Agreement on validation methods (C13, C78-C82). Both evaluations support the rigorous validation and statistical methods. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of correlation coefficients and sample sizes, while peer reviewers characterize methodology as 'solid' without specific concerns.

Agreement on methodological choices (C83-C88). Both evaluations support these documented methods. OpenEval notes the 80% gender probability threshold as reasonable but introducing uncertainty, while peer reviewers accept the methodology as 'solid' overall.

Agreement on prior literature context (C7-C10). Both evaluations support these citations establishing study context. OpenEval notes proper attribution to prior work, while peer reviewers accept the work as 'a valuable addition to the literature.'

Agreement on literature contextualization (C56-C65). Both evaluations support the appropriate citation and representation of prior literature. OpenEval assesses citations as accurate and relevant, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the scholarly context.

Agreement on policy literature (C71-C74). Both evaluations support these citations to COPE guidelines and journal policy literature. OpenEval notes they provide important context for discussion, while peer reviewers accept the overall literature integration.
